opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I should clarify the premise a bit, though. Tim Rocktäschel isn't someone I've worked with inside a company of mine. As far as I know, he's been at Google DeepMind and UCL, and I don't want to invent a working relationship that didn't exist.

What I can speak to is how I see his work from the outside, as someone in the same research community. Tim has been one of the strongest voices for open-endedness: the idea that AI systems shouldn't only optimize a fixed objective but should keep generating new, increasingly complex challenges and capabilities for themselves. His group's work on procedurally generated environments, on NetHack as a research testbed, and on curricula that co-evolve with the agent has been very influential. It pushed a lot of people, including me, to think harder about where the training signal comes from once you've exhausted static datasets.

That question matters a lot to me personally. Much of my own work has been about understanding why these models learn what they learn, and about reasoning and planning. Open-endedness asks the complementary question: how do you keep a system improving when there's no obvious next target? I think the two perspectives fit together well.

So I'd describe his contribution as being to the field rather than to any company of mine, and it's a significant one. If you're asking about collaborators on something I'm building now, I'm happy to talk about that, but I'd rather be accurate than give you a nice-sounding story.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should clarify one thing first: Tim was never formally part of what I'm doing now. He's at Google DeepMind, leading their open-endedness work. But I understand why you'd ask, because our paths overlapped quite a bit when we were both at Meta, at FAIR, and his thinking has really shaped how I look at things.

What Tim brought, and I think this is underappreciated, is a kind of stubbornness about the right problem. A lot of us in that era were chasing benchmarks, pushing numbers on static datasets. Tim kept insisting that intelligence is not something you measure on a fixed test. It's something that emerges when an agent faces an environment that keeps generating new challenges. The NetHack Learning Environment came out of that. People laughed a little at first, a 1980s text roguelike as a frontier benchmark? But it turned out to be exactly the kind of problem where you can't memorize your way through, you have to actually reason and generalize, and it is still hard today.

The second thing is his framing of open-endedness. The idea that you want systems that can keep producing novel and learnable things, not just solve what you handed them. Now that we're all talking about agents, long-horizon reasoning, self-improvement, that framing sounds obvious. It wasn't obvious five or six years ago.

So in terms of contribution to my work, I'd say it's more intellectual than organizational. When I think about how a model should explore, or how to build training environments that don't saturate, I'm often arguing with Tim in my head. We still talk from time to time. We disagree on details, how much structure you bake in versus how much you let emerge, but I'd rather have that argument with him than agree with almost anyone else.
